articles.description: On the frontlines of healthcare, and the strategy table. A cool July afternoon at the Wellcome Collection with the Zimbabwean-British doctor and founder of the women's-health venture Glacie Health, on calling, on education as a form of medicine, and on carrying what the West knows back home to the women who need it.

articles.title: Zimbabwe's tobacco anchor in Britain holds at £129m
articles.description: Of every £100 of goods Zimbabwe sells to Britain, £96 is tobacco or beverages. While the wider UK–Zimbabwe trade relationship softened in the year to December 2025, Zimbabwean tobacco held its grip, and the IMF projects Zimbabwean GDP growth of 7.5% in 2025 and 5.0% in 2026. The product that built Zimbabwe's name as an exporter is still doing the work.

more.title: The Apple of haircare gets its German cheque
more.description: Ruka, the London-based textured-hair company founded by Zimbabwean entrepreneur Varaidzo Tendai Moyo and her co-founder Ugorji Agbai, has closed a $4.5m round co-led by Henkel Ventures and Freedom Trail Capital. The deal, which takes lifetime funding to roughly $10m and brings one of the world's largest consumer-goods groups onto the cap table, is the most meaningful endorsement yet of a Zimbabwean diaspora-founded brand.

more.title: Pardon Mapondera: gone but not forgotten at Venice
more.description: The fifth and final piece in our series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Pardon Mapondera, the artist whose practice the room finally arranges itself around, treats discarded plastic and glass jars not as ecological signal but as ritual matter, and produces, in the process, the most quietly devotional installation in the Biennale this year.

more.title: Gideon Gomo: from stone to bronze, the ancestral algorithm at Venice
more.description: The fourth in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Gideon Gomo's first sustained body of bronze work, paired with discarded vehicle number plates and Zimbabwean springstone, is the move of a sculptor at full maturity rethinking the material vocabulary of his country's most internationally legible art form.

more.title: Shumba Maasai in Venice
more.description: At the 61st Biennale, the Zimbabwean artist's day-long procession through the city's campi, performed under the borrowed authority of a Murehwa chief, restages the social-sculpture lineage of Joseph Beuys for a contemporary African discursive practice.

more.title: Franklyn Dzingai: family albums and the neural commons at Venice
more.description: The third in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Franklyn Dzingai's reductive cardboard prints, built from the family album, the magazine clipping, the back-room studio photographs of mid-century Zimbabwe, turn out, on close looking, to be the most precisely engineered work in the room.

more.title: Felix Shumba: charcoal and the practice of disappearance at Venice
more.description: The second in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Felix Shumba's six-metre charcoal wall and his Telephone Reader series anchor a body of work that argues drawing is not the act of capturing the seen, but the act of staying present to what is on its way out of sight.

more.title: UK services share in Zimbabwe rises to 8.2%
more.description: The headline UK services trade with Zimbabwe softened year on year. The structural number underneath it tells the better story: Britain's share of all services Zimbabwe imports rose 2.4 percentage points to 8.2%, the highest measured level in years. As Zimbabwean buyers re-rate their global supplier mix, the UK is taking a bigger slice of the country's services demand.

more.title: Zimbabwe's demand lifts British exports by 14.6%
more.description: The Zimbabwean economy is in its strongest stretch in years: 7.5% GDP growth in 2025, a projected 5% in 2026, and that growth is pulling demand for cars, commercial vehicles, medicines and industrial machinery in with it. UK goods exports to Zimbabwe rose 14.6% on the year, the strongest line in an otherwise soft bilateral picture for Britain.

more.title: Experts urge stronger support for breastfeeding mothers
more.description: Amos Mpofu and Sikhulekelani Moyo, Zimpapers Reporters ZIMBABWE has joined more than 170 countries in commemorating World Breastfeeding Week, which began on Saturday and runs until August 7, with health experts calling for stronger family, workplace and community support systems to enable mothers to breastfeed successfully and improve child survival and development. This year's global theme, Breastfeeding for a Sustainable Start in Life: Strengthen What Works, highlights the need to protect, promote and support breastfeeding as one of the most effective interventions for improving maternal and child health. Observed annually from August 1 to 7, World Breastfeeding Week is led by the World Alliance for Breastfeeding Action (WABA) in collaboration with the World Health Organisation (WHO), UNICEF and other partners. The campaign seeks to raise awareness of the lifelong health benefits of breastfeeding while encouraging governments, employers, healthcare providers and communities to create environments that enable mothers to breastfeed. President of the Paediatric Association of Zimbabwe, Dr Nyashadzashe Chasauka, said breastfeeding is one of the most powerful public health interventions available to reduce child mortality and promote healthy growth and development. Breastfeeding is the most important foundation in a child's life, which is why Breastfeeding Week is an important week in our health calendar as it raises awareness on the importance of breastfeeding and advocates for support for breastfeeding mothers, he said. Breastfeeding is a strong start for a healthy and sustainable future for the baby and a mother's milk is the first best gift of life. Breast milk is nutritious and protects babies from diarrhoeal diseases, chest infections and ear infections. Dr Chasauka said breastfeeding not only improves a child's chances of survival during infancy but also contributes to healthier growth, stronger immunity and better development throughout life. According to the World Health Organisation, babies should be exclusively breastfed for the first six months, after which nutritious complementary foods should be introduced while breastfeeding continues until at least two years of age or beyond. Exclusive breastfeeding means infants receive only breast milk, without water, other liquids or foods, except prescribed medicines or vitamin supplements where necessary. Dr Chasauka also encouraged mothers living with HIV to breastfeed, saying modern treatment has significantly reduced the risk of mother-to-child transmission. All mothers can breastfeed, including mothers who are living with HIV. Mothers living with HIV need to adhere to their ARV treatment and babies given prophylactic medication during breastfeeding to prevent mother-to-child transmission, he said. Paediatrician and child health specialist Dr Wedu Ndebele said breastfeeding offers long-term health benefits that extend well beyond infancy. He said breastfed children are less likely to suffer from allergies, asthma and certain skin conditions while studies have also linked breastfeeding to improved brain development and cognitive performance. I hope everyone will talk about breastfeeding this week and encourage whether it's your sister, your mother or your wife to breastfeed for the first six months without giving anything. We also encourage them to breastfeed up to two years of age if there's no contraindication because those babies will grow very well, said Dr Ndebele. Registered nutritionist Ms Katinka Musavaya urged mothers experiencing breastfeeding difficulties to seek professional support instead of abandoning breastfeeding prematurely. Nourishing your baby from your breast is a powerful way to give them a strong start in life. No medicine, food or supplement is so perfectly crafted to suit your individual baby in your unique environment, and it's free too, she said. Breastfeeding is natural, but it can also be exhausting and challenging. With the right support, you can overcome the hard days and feel confident in your breastfeeding journey. Ms Musavaya also expressed concern over increasing marketing of infant formula products, warning that aggressive advertising often undermines exclusive breastfeeding. She called for stricter enforcement of the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes, which seeks to regulate the promotion of infant formula and protect breastfeeding. We urge strict enforcement of the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes, and caution families that formula marketing is designed to sell a product, not to reflect medical necessity, she said. Nutritionist Mrs Annie Msauki Busumani said frequent breastfeeding, both day and night, is essential for establishing and maintaining an adequate milk supply. Breastfeeding day and night, on demand and without restricting frequency, is one of the most effective ways to build and sustain a mother's milk supply. In our work with mothers across Zimbabwe, we have seen this simple, evidence-based practice work again and again, especially in those critical early weeks when supply is being established, she said. She said adolescent and teenage mothers often face unique challenges, including fear of disclosing their pregnancies, pressure from families and the need to return to school, factors that sometimes lead to mixed feeding instead of seeking professional guidance. Dietitian Ms Portia Chisvo said breastfeeding remains the gold standard for infant nutrition while also benefiting mothers. Breastfeeding gives babies the best nutrition and protection, and helps mothers recover too. Feed exclusively for the first six months, on demand with a good latch. Then continue with complementary foods up to two years and beyond. It's nutrition, immunity and bonding all in one, she said. Zimbabwe has made significant progress in promoting exclusive breastfeeding through the Ministry of Health and Child Care, Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative and community-based nutrition programmes. Health authorities continue to encourage early initiation of breastfeeding within the first hour after birth and exclusive breastfeeding for six months as part of efforts to reduce child mortality, malnutrition and stunting.
